subject: Biotechnology
title: Enzymatic Textile Waste Recycling
description: A micro-lesson that makes Enzymatic Textile Waste Recycling usable.

hook.text: 92 million tons of textiles are discarded annually — enzymes can separate blended fibers that mechanical recycling cannot handle.

buildup.text: Cellulase enzymes selectively digest cotton in cotton-polyester blends — leaving clean polyester fibers for recycling.

discovery.text: Protease enzymes break down wool and silk — recovering amino acids for new materials without harsh chemical processing.

twist.text: Dyes and finishes interfere with enzymatic digestion — pretreatment to remove chemicals adds cost and complexity.

climax.text: Carbios and Worn Again Technologies scale enzymatic textile recycling — closing the loop on fashion's waste crisis.

punchline.text: Enzymes untangle your old clothes — biological recycling separates what machines cannot.

quiz.question: Why are enzymes useful for recycling blended fabrics?
options: They can melt both natural and synthetic fibers simultaneously
They selectively digest one fiber type like cotton while leaving the other like polyester intact for recycling
They permanently remove all dyes and make fabrics reusable

details.summary: Enzymes break down textile waste into reusable raw materials, separating blended fabrics and depolymerizing fibers that conventional recycling cannot process. Cellulases, proteases, and engineered PET hydrolases can disassemble clothing into chemical building blocks for new fabric production.
details.whyItMatters: The fashion industry produces 92 million tons of textile waste annually, with most going to landfills. Enzymatic recycling can process blended fabrics that mechanical recycling cannot separate, enabling true circular fashion material flows.
takeaways: Enzymes can separate cotton-polyester blends that mechanical recycling cannot
Engineered PET hydrolases break polyester back into its chemical monomers
Enzymatic processes operate at mild conditions with lower environmental impact

faq.question: Why is textile recycling so difficult today?
faq.answer: Most clothing contains fiber blends like cotton-polyester that cannot be mechanically separated. Dyes, finishes, and elastane further complicate processing. Less than 1 percent of clothing is recycled into new clothing. Current methods mostly shred textiles into low-value insulation or rags.

faq.question: How do enzymes separate blended fabric materials?
faq.answer: Cellulases selectively digest cotton fibers from cotton-polyester blends, leaving pure polyester behind. The polyester can then be processed separately. Alternatively, PET hydrolases break polyester into monomers while leaving natural fibers intact. Each enzyme targets its specific fiber type.
